newsitem.title: USA: Tougher US rules needed to prevent mad cow - author.
newsitem.headline: Tougher US rules needed to prevent mad cow - author.

text.p: Proposed Food and Drug Administration rules to ban the use of cattle brains, spinal columns and other remains to make animal feed don't go far enough to protect meat-eating consumers, Pulitzer Prize-winning author Richard Rhodes said in an interview.
"The issue clearly is whether we're going to decide to ban the use of all animal remains in all animal feed," he said. "Nothing less than that will work."

The U.S. meat packing industry contends that an end to recycling animal waste into feed for other animals could cost $1.6 billion annually in disposing of the unused remains. Other trade groups have downplayed the proposed rules, calling them an extra precaution against the so-called "mad cow" disease.
Rhodes this month published "Deadly Feast", a book which traces the history of the so-called "mad cow" disease and the risks to the meat-eating public of recycling animal remains.
Some 17 deaths in Britain and France have been blamed so far on an outbreak of mad cow disease, known to scientists as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
No deaths or animal contamination have been reported in the United States, which banned British beef imports.

Mad cow disease is one type of a group of deadly brain diseases known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies that slowly eat tiny holes in the brain. Victims lose control of their muscles, become demented and lose the ability to swallow. There is no cure.

Rhodes, who won a Pulitzer Prize in 1988 for his book, "The Making of the Atomic Bomb," contends that Britain's experience shows how rapidly human food can be infected when animal remains are recycled.

British scientists eventually determined that the disease was spread through the practice of recycling animal rendering wastes -- including brains, spinal cords and other unsaleable remains -- into protein supplements fed to cattle.
"The public isn't aware of how much waste material is recycled," Rhodes said. "This is a fact about the way our food is prepared and we need to open a dialogue with the industry."

In January, the FDA proposed new regulations to outlaw the feeding of processed animal wastes known as ruminants to cattle. But although U.S. regulators and industry groups believe the proposed rules are adequate to prevent mad cow disease, Rhodes says tougher measures are needed.

"That would be enough if we could be confident that the ban on feeding ruminants is going to be properly enforced in this country," Rhodes said. "But the British example doesn't make for a lot of confidence. There's been a good deal of cheating on the ban by continuing to use animal remains to make feed."
And the FDA proposal doesn't prohibit feeding ruminants to pigs or chickens, which could serve as other pathways to spread the disease, he said.
The USDA already set up a computer database to collect data about animal health conditions and trained U.S. veterinarians to be on alert for any signs of the disease.

The National Cattlemen's Beef Association said Rhodes' new book fails to present scientific evidence, especially from the USDA which has been monitoring the disease for a decade. USDA scientists have examined the brains of more than 5,000 U.S. cattle since 1986 and found no evidence of mad cow disease.

"It appears that BSE (mad cow disease) does not exist here," said Dick Weiss of the National Milk Producers Federation. "We believe that the reason for the FDA to issue a proposed ban on ruminant feed is just an extra precaution and not an admission of BSE (mad cow disease)."
"I'm not trying to scaremonger. I'm trying to report the scientific literature as I found it and open a dialogue," Rhodes said.
"The fact the FDA is proposing this rule recognises that there is a real possibility of contamination. The real issue is whether or not we're going to stop it before it spreads in our country."
